utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too. Just to inform the public, we are starting late because we had some technical glitches which fortunately have now been sorted out. Are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are. May I ask that we go into private session for the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Your Honours know, when we last met last week, I had a very brief opportunity to look at the report given that it was only supplied in full on, I believe, Monday -- I think we've had it just over a week. Your Honour, I'm raising at this stage the question of what this evidence, the relevance of this evidence at all. Your Honour, having gone through the report, it was said in the part of Mr. Ackerman's submissions on witnesses that Professor -- or Mr. Shoup would be called. He was the co-author of the book "The War in Bosnia and Herzegovina" which is in evidence as DB1. He will discuss the conclusions in the book and will review and discuss the testimonies of Donia and Treanor, and he will prepare a report based on these and other materials. Now, Your Honour, first of all, there's one reference to Dr. Donia in the whole of this report. If Your Honour turns to page 14, when he says, "The report of the expert witness for the Prosecution, Professor Donia," he's actually a doctor, but I'm sure he won't mind being promoted, "...has touched on the issue of how the Serbs of Bosanska Krajina asserted their independence from the government in Sarajevo." Well, he does more than that. But we would like to fill in the picture supplied by Professor Donia, but have chosen not to do so in this report, lacking an account of the emergence of national movements in the Bosanska Krajina region. So in other words, this author or this witness does not dispute what Dr. Donia has said, and indeed nowhere in the report is there any direct contradiction or report of anything that Dr. Donia said. Mr. Treanor's report is never even mentioned. I don't know whether he ever read it or looked at it. But there's no mention of it, and certainly there's nothing to suggest that anything that Mr. Treanor had to say was inaccurate or misconceived or anything of that nature. Your Honour, what the report deals with in some detail is international negotiations of which the Court has already heard evidence, and then turns to deal with areas of Bosnia about which this Court has heard absolutely no evidence. For example, a great deal of time is spent on the Sarajevo and the marketplace bombings. Your Honour, I'm reinforced in that by the exhibits that Mr. Ackerman finally -- we had real difficulty in working out what it was from this huge Dutch report Mr. Ackerman was going to refer to. But he has now given us copies. If Your Honours look at what is marked DB364A, which is history and reminders in East Bosnia. Now, unless I'm very much mistaken, this Court has been dealing with northwest Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 364A, headed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 364A, what I have is Appendix 4. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: History and reminders of East Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 365A is also history and reminders of East Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a continuation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't the faintest idea. It's a very odd report, but it's different in any event because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because even 369 is history and reminders in East Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a very oddly structured website. Because both say chapter 4, and both say under communist rule, but they're different. And Your Honour, that's one of the problems we had. But can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're referring to 364 anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am. Srebrenica in Tito's time. Your Honour, gripping though that may be, and I did manage to -- or rather Ms. Gustin managed to extract that one from the website, it has absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with any of the issues that Your Honours are considering. And this, I understand, is an exhibit that Professor Shoup is going to be asked to look at. Your Honour, one of the rules of admissibility of evidence, and particularly where it comes to a Defence expert, is that it must be relevant to issues that the Court has to decide and issues that are in dispute in this case. Now, at the moment, I am unaware of what it is precisely that this report of Professor Shoup, (a), is supposed to contradict in whatever Dr. Donia and Mr. Treanor said; and (b), how a ramble round Srebrenica under communist rule is going to help Your Honours at all. So Your Honour, I'm merely raising at this stage for Mr. Ackerman to explain to me, perhaps, and to the Court how this report and this evidence is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure this objection is even very well placed. I first -- I know you don't have with you the report of Dr. Donia, but I suppose I could argue that all the stuff in Dr. Donia's report about Habsburg rule and the mountain wreath and what happened in 1847 and the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement, and I could go on and on about stuff in this report of Donia that may not be relevant. But I think it is. I don't think you can get a grasp of what happened in Bosnia in this war in 1992 if you don't have a grasp of some background, some history, because what happened -- you know, people act out of their past. They act out of what they know from the past. They act out of history. So you need to understand that history. The concept of how is anything that happened in Srebrenica relevant? Well, I think I can show you how it is, if you will just listen to Professor Shoup testify. And you have in the record in this case, Your Honour, thousands of documents which I have objected on relevance. And your response, I think, is correct in terms of the law, we're going to sort that out at the end of this case. And so I think you need to do is listen to this evidence, and if you find that some of its not relevant to your consideration, then sort it out at the end of the case. But I believe it's all relevant or I wouldn't be putting it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty is at this stage, is this: That I appreciate Dr. Donia set the background, but nothing in what is contained in Professor Shoup's report suggests that what Dr. Donia said is in any way wrong. And therefore, Your Honours have heard that evidence. And as I say, one of the rules is it is unnecessary to hear further evidence on matters which are not in dispute. In respect of documents, Your Honour, at no stage were any of the documents objected to on grounds of relevance, but more on grounds of authenticity or whatever because at no stage have we sought to put in to this case documents which don't in some way directly relate to the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina or the greater part, which goes to the joint criminal enterprise. Now, Your Honour, all I say is this: Your Honours may, of course, sit and listen to Mr. Ackerman explaining through Professor Shoup how this is relevant, but it does open and it will open, I'm afraid, areas outside those which Your Honours have considered so far and will have to consider for the judgement. As I say, Your Honours what we're about to hear from -- if the report is to be made an exhibit, we're going to go into details of the marketplace massacre in Sarajevo, about which there has already been a trial. And -- just a moment, Mr. Ackerman, let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's no good Mr. Ackerman saying no. He may not be taking Dr. Shoup through it, but it's there in the report which will be an exhibit in the case. The report has not been edited in any way, and so therefore we have to deal with matters that are in evidence, whether directly addressed by the witness or in a document that becomes an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I've said all I need to say. I believe I've responded. The only thing I was getting up to say was that we're not going into the Mahala marketplace thing. That's clearly not relevant to any issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's just made my point for me. What part of this report is relevant? But you can't just put in irrelevant matters in a document which is part of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But on the other hand, Ms. Korner, let's grant you, for the sake of argument, that there are bits and pieces or parts of this report which deal with matters or events which are completely irrelevant. What's your solution? Strike the entire report because of some irrelevant material contained in it, if it contains other events and other considerations which are fundamentally important to the case before us? What do you do?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can tell Your Honours what I would do, but I don't think it would be appropriate. Your Honours, what I'm asking for -- as yet, Mr. Ackerman has given a sort of vague reply that it is relevant, but he hasn't indicated to what issue this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I read you loud and clear actually. But let's discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we've discussed it very briefly. I don't know if you could hear what we were saying, but more or less the position is as follows, Ms. Korner, Mr. Ackerman: We believe that we should not dissect the report pre-emptively before we have even started hearing the testimony of Professor Shoup. Our position is that the report should be looked at in its entirety as a whole, as a -- holistically, and if at any time in the course of his testimony you would like to ask Professor Shoup about relevant parts of his report, but it's up to you. I mean, you will be free to do it. We may do the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely I appreciate that. All I can say is that Your Honours won't then be stopping me exploring areas of this report about which I have to -- I wish to cross-examine but which have absolutely nothing to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're following into a contradiction because you're saying you want to go deeper into areas which you consider to be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, you are letting in what, I submit, and Your Honours overruled me, a report which we would submit is irrelevant to any issue that Your Honours need to decide. Once that's in, then I take it Your Honours will not be stopping me from cross-examining on any areas that are outside the ambit of this case because this is what this report covers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will hear the questions first, and then we will decide, Ms. Korner. On principle, we are not going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else before we start with Professor Shoup? Am I pronouncing it well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's Shoup, Your Honour. Shoup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Usher, please could you escort Professor Shoup in. Thank you. Incidentally, Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, I see here a number of documents. These I know where they are, because they are the Defence documents. Then I see other documents here. Banja Luka clinical medical centre, the transcript of an intercept. What's this? Are you aware of this, Mr. Ackerman? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Banja Luka Medical Centre documents are the documents that we had suggested we were trying to get regarding the 12 dead babies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. These are yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The intercept that you see was one that simply early in the case we realised it had the wrong names where it showed someone else speaking when it was actually Karadzic. That has just been corrected. Ms. Gustin told me earlier about it today, so I'm familiar with it and happy with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That explains it then. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it these documents dealing with the children, the oxygen babies, are you going to be dealing with those documents today? No. So we can put them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. We'll not deal with those at all. Just at the close of the Defence case, I'll offer them as exhibits, Your Honour, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Good afternoon, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it your first time here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been here simply as an observer and as a backup to Professor Vladimiroff, four or five years ago at the time of the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So welcome once more. I'll be very brief. You are about to start giving evidence as an expert witness for the Defence. Before you do so, our Rules require that you enter an solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony you will be telling us the truth. The text is contained in the paper that the usher -- Mr. Usher is going to hand to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please read that aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just give me one moment, please. Just put these things that may come in handy here in front of me. There we go. Excuse me. It's the first time. Is that sufficient? Can you hear me? Please, I'm ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You're going first to be asked questions by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whom you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he will then be followed -- I don't know exactly when, whether it will be this week or next week. He will be followed by Ms. Korner, who is the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. Is she here? Could she identify herself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no way of knowing otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not in the habit of doing this, but I am actually Ms. Korner, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good. It helps me to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your name is Paul Shoup?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are a retired professor of political science from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, Virginia, USA?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You received your B.A. with Honours from Swarthmore College?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You then studied at the Russian Institute at Columbia University?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Law Faculty of Belgrade University?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Department of Public Law and Government at Columbia University?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where you received your doctorate in 1960.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your doctoral dissertation was entitled, "Communism and the National Question in Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please make breaks before question and answer. Interpreters can't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Shoup. There is a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, and I apologise. And I will be more careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You taught at Kenyon College from 1960 until 1963?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then spend the rest of your teaching career at University of Virginia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You received fellowships and grants from Fulbright Hayes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Ford Foundation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: IREX, which stands for International Research and Exchanges Board?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the National Council for Soviet and East European Research?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were a Olin Fellow at Harvard university in 1989?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A fellow at the international programme for advanced international studies at the federal institution for east European and international studies in Cologne, Germany, in 1989?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a visiting scholar at Radio Free Europe in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You served twice as director of Centre for Russian and East European Studies at the University of Virginia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also served as president of the American Association for Southeast European Studies between 1985 and 1989?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your dissertation was also published by Columbia University Press?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are the editor of "Problems of Balkan Security: Southeastern Europe in the 1990s" published in 1990?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are the editor of "Bosnia Between War and Peace" published in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct, in Serbo-Croatian, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are co-editor of the "Yugoslav War, Europe and the Balkans" published in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are also the co-author, along with Professor Steven Burg of Brandeis University of the study "The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina: Ethnic Conflict and International Intervention" published in 1999?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that is the book that you have there with you which is --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- also DB1, Exhibit DB1 in this case. And this book won the Ralph J. Bunche award of the American Political Science Association for the year 2000 for the best scholarly work in political science which explores the phenomenon of ethnic and cultural pluralism?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Over the last few days, you have had an opportunity, have you not, to review a couple of videos that we have shown you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know the two videos that I'm referring to? They are two segments of a documentary. They are denominated for the record in this case as DB358 and DB359?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: I presume you're referring to the "Avoidable War".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sorry. So hard at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before we begin presenting the videos to the Chamber, do you agree with all the conclusions reached in this documentary?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The basic premise of the documentary seems to be this: That if the Germans had not prematurely --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I don't think we'll have counsel giving evidence, thank you. Your Honours can see the video. As to what the basic premise is, Your Honours will be make up your own minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I personally have no idea what video you're talking about, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They were given to you last week, Your Honour. You were given two CDs with the videos on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Those are the ones. How am I supposed to know which one you're referring to? Which one are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's actually both of them, Your Honour. There are two. They are DB358 and DB35 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's refer specifically to which part of the video you're questioning the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there's two ways to do this. I can do it now or wait till it comes up in the video. Either way all I'm trying to do is show that there's a portion of it that he doesn't really agree with. I can do that many ways. I don't care how we do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness can say, as Mr. Ackerman keeps pointing out to me, it's not for counsel to give evidence. The witness can watch the videos, and he can say what parts he doesn't agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. I'm perfectly willing to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the proper way to go about it. Alternatively, if you have some particular part or excerpt of that video which you have reason to believe that the witness may or may not agree upon, you just point him directly to that part. But we need to be put in a position to be able to follow, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, even though you've told us that you disagree with some portions of the video, do you believe it can assist this Trial Chamber, and in some cases amplify and explain your own testimony to be given later?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I support that position. I think it shows that, first of all, that there are many leading experts who are shown in the video who felt at the time of the crisis in Yugoslavia that the question of the Serbs outside of Serbia proper was a very difficult and complex question, that it could not be reduced down to a simple proposition that Milosevic was waging an aggressive war for a Greater Serbia. I won't say that these experts were right or wrong, but you will see that they are very reputable and knowledgeable people who have a great deal of experience and who are looking at this war from a much more complicated point of view than sometimes the media was at the time. The other thing I think -- and I'll be quick about it -- is simply that it shows you what the Serbs in Croatia and in Bosnia, too, were thinking. It shows you how they viewed this conflict. It's really very hard to get inside their minds and to see what they were thinking, and the shock that this situation had on them at the time. This film, this documentary is partly propaganda, let's face it, but it does show you in a very emotional, vivid way how these people were viewing what was going around them. So I don't think it's a very important documentary for the Court to see, if they haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose now to begin running the video. And we'll stop it on occasions for questions I might have or questions. If you have questions, you can stop it. And Professor Shoup will stop it occasionally to make comments also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it should be on your screen on the computer evidence button. And if everybody can see it, as soon as everybody is comfortable with starting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply a question, do I say to you "stop"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, if there's something you want to comment on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.text: This is such a crucial moment in the history of the breakup of Yugoslavia that I feel it's necessary to say a word or two, and I apologise to the Judges if you have been over this many, many times before. But there is a little bit of misleading information here in the documentary, and it helps us to understand what's going on later in Bosnia. Here we have a situation, first of all, where the European conference under Lord Carrington has proposed that the six republics of Yugoslavia form six independent states loosely tied in a confederation. They insist that the borders of Croatia should remain where they are, although they also insist that Zagreb should provide autonomy for the Serbs within Croatia. Over the course of the fall of 1991, these points are debated, including the fate of Kosovo. In the end, this is now November of 1991, Milosevic stays firm on the position that the Serbs of Croatia have the right to self-determination. He's willing to accept practically -- virtually everything that the European Community proposes. But his insistence on the right of self-determination for the Serbs of Croatia means ultimately that the borders of Croatia are not sacrosanct and therefore that the -- some basic principles of the European Union's proposals are being, in effect, violated. Now, it should be noted that the European Union stuck to its position with German support all the way through October 1991. The Germans did not defect from this common European position. And this common European position was that no single ex-Yugoslav republic could be recognised and given official recognition until there was a comprehensive settlement of the problems that had arisen as a result of the disintegration of Yugoslavia. And the reason for this was very simple, and that is that Lord Carrington, leading the negotiations, felt that recognition was the only tool that he had in order to force these respective republics to make a concession here or a concession there that would lead to a compromise and finally a peaceful outcome of the discussions. Finally, in December of 1991, after Milosevic had made clear that he was going to remain adamant about the right of self-determination for the Serbs in Croatia did Genscher, then, proclaim on December 8th that Germany had decided that it would recognise simply two republics instead of all of them, namely Croatia and Slovenia. Lord Carrington was very upset by this. He felt that the one tool that he had to force a compromise on the republics, that is, the right of recognition, was being taken away from him. And he was also very upset because he felt that this was a provocative act, and it could lead to renewed fighting at a higher level in Croatia by the Serbs who would respond to this move, and he was afraid, as well, that if Croatia and Slovenia were recognised, that Bosnia would be recognised soon after. And I might continue just for a minute or two, if we can break off my narrative right now, or we can continue this for another five minutes so we can see how this all works itself out, and perhaps the latter way would be the best way to do it. Remember that at this particular point, that the Americans also are against the recognition of Croatia, so that the Americans and the Germans are on the same side. Now, the Americans have not participated in the conference at The Hague right here, the EEC conference we have been talking about, but they are allying themselves with Lord Carrington's position -- I'm sorry, I've made a mistake. The Americans are against recognition. They are allying themselves with Lord Carrington's position, not with the German position; I apologise. Let's back up a little bit. I see a little confusion on the faces of some of the Judges.

I don't think that their motives were identical to those of Lord Carrington's. They, the Americans, were not really interested in a negotiated solution within the framework of the EC conference. They would have welcomed it, but they weren't interested. Rather, they were convinced that the nub of the problem lay in the aggressive intentions of Slobodan Milosevic. And because they were afraid of Milosevic, they were afraid that recognition of Croatia would lead to a reaction by the Serbs, that they would attack, perhaps even occupy Zagreb, let's say hypothetically, and would attack Bosnia as well. And this was a crucial moment in the coming apart of Yugoslavia because by December of 1991, the Serbs had agreed that they would pull their troops out of those areas of Croatia which had been taken over by the Serb minority, and in their place, place a UN force, the UNPROFOR. So there was a truce momentarily in Croatia, and at the same time a civil war had not taken on a violent turn yet in Bosnia. This was an opportunity, then, in November, December, and January of 1992 to try to find some kind an overall solution to the problem of the disintegration of Yugoslavia. Let me just briefly tell you what happened, because it's very interesting, and it's a comedy of errors in a way because things never worked out the way they were supposed to. On the one hand, the fears that Zimmerman, in particular I think, had that Milosevic would engage in aggressive actions as a consequence of this recognition --

And I mention this in particular because after this had occurred, we can safely infer, because this is nowhere in the memoirs of Warren Zimmerman or anywhere else, we can safely infer that Warren Zimmerman decided at this point that, in fact, the Germans were right, that they had done the right thing in recognising Croatia, that Milosevic had become more reasonable as a consequence, and then in turn the Americans decided in the spring of 1992 that they would apply the same tactic, which I might just liberally call pre-emptive recognition, that they would apply the same tactic of pre-emptive recognition to Bosnia, expecting the same results that had occurred in Croatia. In fact, of course, this did not happen, and they had completely misread Milosevic's intentions in this respect. This leads us into the spring of 1992 when there might have been a window in which to negotiate some kind of a peaceful resolution of all of these complicated problems. But I'll stop here. The purpose of what I am doing is to try to show you how extremely complex that situation was in the fall of 1991. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And in the meantime, I think Professor Shoup has got -- if I could read him, where he has got some information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, first of all, I do have that original myself. I hadn't seen it for some time. I would be glad to provide it for the Court. I can get Mrs. Shoup to send it to us. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to correct the record in this respect, these negotiations which took place in July of 1991 and are analysed in the book, "The War in Bosnia Herzegovina" did not come to fruition in part because Izetbegovic and the Muslim side insisted that if Bosnia was to remain in Yugoslavia or in what in Serbo-Croatian it would be called "krnja" Yugoslavia and which I call rump Yugoslavia for -- because of lack of a better word, if Bosnia was to remain in Yugoslavia, Croatia would also have to be part of that Yugoslavia. And of course, by this time, in July of 1991, it was clear that that was impossible. And as we go along, and as my report to the Court has indicated, this was a point which just could not be resolved. The insistence of Bosnia -- of Izetbegovic that they would not join a rump Yugoslavia unless Croatia was part of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop. Again, I apologise. Maybe Mr. Ackerman should give the...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're at 53.40 basically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult here in Court to clarify what are obviously very complex, murky relationships, but I want to make one remark. Let us remember that on March 10th of 1992 in Brussels, the United States and the Europeans agreed that Bosnia would be recognised by April 6th. Now, that meant for the Bosnians, that is, for Izetbegovic, that there was absolutely no reason for him to make any concessions during the course of the Cutileiro negotiations which followed March 10th. Otherwise, he might jeopardise what was his only hope for salvation, which was recognition of Bosnia, military assistance or whatever might follow. So that the discussion we see here is in some ways beside the point. Izetbegovic could clearly see that at this point it was not in his interests if Bosnia was to survive for him to make any concessions and become involved in lengthy negotiations and put off -- and put off recognition.

utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm sorry. The Serbs themselves made claims during the war that they owned something like 60 per cent of the land. This was a distortion because they were referring to land -- much of the land was owned by the government and was not private, so their claim for 60 per cent of the land might have really only related to, you know, privately owned land which could have been any percentage of the total. At the same time, if you -- as we note in the book, there are maps that have been drawn on the basis of what they call the cadastre, the agricultural acre, so to speak. And if -- that's a more detailed map of Bosnia and of who owns what. And in that case, the Serb claim that they owned over 50 per cent of the land is confirmed, but certainly not 70 per cent of the land. So this is just some little background on this ongoing debate and how much land the Serbs did occupy, but they certainly occupied more than 33 or 40 per cent of the land.

utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've learned that the BBC reporter we've seen -- that you identified as a BBC reporter, his name is Nick Gowing, I believe.

utterances.text: Do you now know who this is?

utterances.text: We're at 14.54, I think now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: Do you know this person at all?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I can't identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Can we go back. This is the BBC -- do you recognise him now? Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with luck I think we'll be able to stop guessing like mad when we get the proper tape.
